Part 1

Arc Hydro: what and why

Why water resources work needs a structured GIS framework

Why Arc Hydro?

Key idea

Hydrologic systems are spatial and interconnected. Arc Hydro gives a structured way to analyze them.

Water resource managers use it to

  • Incorporate spatial features
  • Execute spatial analyses:
    • Assessing water quality
    • Estimating water availability
    • Planning flood prevention
    • Investigating watershed health
    • Managing water resources

It lets you

  • Integrate raster data (DEMs, precipitation) with vector data (streams, boundaries)
  • Build relationships between them

How watershed characteristics influence discharge, Q (Q = velocity × area)

  • Topography controls slope, flow velocity and drainage direction
  • Shape: elongated vs. circular watersheds change the timing of peak flow
  • Size: larger watersheds usually have delayed, attenuated hydrographs
  • Soil type: infiltration capacity vs. runoff generation
  • Land use: urban impervious surfaces increase runoff

Decisions this supports

Floodplain mapping, infrastructure design, climate change impact assessment

What is Arc Hydro? (1) A data model

Key idea

Arc Hydro is a template data model for water resources: it defines what features exist and how they relate.

What the template does

  • Links hydrologic data to modeling and decision-support tools
  • Standardizes data structure, making it consistent, efficient, spatial and expandable

Relationships it defines

  • A stream segment has a corresponding catchment
  • Multiple catchments combine into a watershed
  • Each watershed has an outlet point

Why a standard matters

It supports hydrologic models, upstream/downstream tracking and network analysis. Without it, datasets may use inconsistent names, lack connectivity information, and be hard to bring into models.

What is Arc Hydro? (2) A packaged set of GIS tools

Key idea

The tools automate hydrologic workflows, turning raster DEMs into connected vector features: streams, catchments, watersheds.

  • Generate and populate a geodatabase with vector or raster data
  • Establish relationships between classes and features
  • Use geometric networks to tie data together
  • Populate attributes
  • Perform tasks like watershed delineation or basin characterization
  • Use XML data exchange to integrate external models
  • Expand or customize the tools for your needs

Key concept: topology

Topology is the set of connectivity rules between features. It:

  • Ensures streams connect correctly
  • Ensures flow moves downstream logically
  • Prevents disconnected or invalid networks

What can you do with Arc Hydro?

Create basemaps

Create basemaps and GIS data that support simulations, e.g. watersheds and stream networks as model inputs.

Integrate data types

Combine hydrologic (drainage), topographic (slope) and topologic (network) data.

Display results

Show simulation results on a map, e.g. flood depths or pollutant concentrations.

Natural + built systems

Integrate natural drainage (streams) with man-made structures (storm drains).

Inspect the data

Reveal overlooked flow conditions (soil or slope changes). Flow going uphill signals a data error.

Example: post-wildfire

Identify burned areas contributing sediment, analyze changed runoff pathways, link land-cover change to hydrologic response.

Check your understanding

Answer in your own words first, then open the answer to check.

Q1 Arc Hydro is described as two things. What are they, and how do they work together?

A data model (defines water features and how they relate) and a toolset (populates the model and builds the features from data such as DEMs).

Q2 Name three watershed characteristics that influence discharge (Q). Explain how one of them changes the hydrograph.

Any three of topography, shape, size, soil, land use. E.g. larger watersheds give delayed, attenuated hydrographs; impervious land use increases runoff.

Q3 What is topology, and why does a stream network need it?

Connectivity rules between features. They keep streams connected, flow moving downstream, and prevent broken or invalid networks.

Part 2

Terrain, DEMs and the D8 idea

How elevation controls where water goes, and how a digital grid of elevations lets us compute it

DEM-based watershed and stream network delineation

Key idea

A DEM is a grid where each cell stores an elevation. If water follows topography, we can derive flow paths from it.

What we derive from a DEM

  • Flow direction: where water flows
  • Flow accumulation: how much water accumulates
  • Stream network: where channels form
  • Watersheds: contributing areas

The D8 assumption

Water flows to the steepest downslope neighbor, one of 8 directions (the eight-direction pour point model).

Limitations

  • Does not capture subsurface flow
  • Simplifies complex flow patterns

Duality between terrain and drainage network

Key idea

Topography and drainage networks co-evolve: water carves valleys, and valleys guide future flow.

Two-way feedback

  • Water erodes the landscape and carries away sediment, sculpting topography
  • Topography defines drainage direction, runoff and flow accumulation

What the feedback creates

  • Dendritic (branching) drainage patterns
  • Organized stream hierarchies

What this means for modeling

We assume the DEM represents this equilibrium, so we can infer flow paths from elevation.

Where the assumption breaks down

  • Urban areas: pipes override topography
  • Recently disturbed landscapes, e.g. post-fire debris flows

Watershed delineation: heads-up digitizing

Key idea

Before DEMs, watersheds were traced by hand on a topographic map: the outlet decides everything.

“Heads-up” digitizing means tracing features on screen over a map.

Read the figure

  • Watershed divide (red line): the highest-elevation boundary
  • Drainage direction (arrows): the path water takes, downhill across contours
  • Outlet: the control point for the analysis

Why the outlet is critical

  • It defines the watershed boundary
  • It is where discharge is calculated

Wrong outlet → wrong watershed → wrong results.

DEM elevations

Key idea

Topo maps became digital: contour lines were replaced by a grid of elevation values.

Manual (contours)

  • Expert interpretation
  • Time-consuming
  • Subjective

DEM-based

  • Automated
  • Reproducible
  • Scalable
Watch out

Automation does not guarantee accuracy. It depends on DEM resolution, data quality and preprocessing.

Check your understanding

Answer in your own words first, then open the answer to check.

Q4 What does the D8 method assume about how water moves? Name one situation where that assumption fails.

Water flows to the steepest downslope of its 8 neighbors (it follows topography). Fails for subsurface flow, urban pipes, splitting flow, recently disturbed landscapes.

Q5 Why is choosing the outlet the most important decision in delineating a watershed?

The outlet defines the boundary and where discharge is computed: a wrong outlet gives a wrong watershed and wrong results.

Q6 Give two advantages of DEM-based delineation over hand delineation, and one factor that still limits its accuracy.

Automated, reproducible, scalable. Still limited by DEM resolution, data quality and preprocessing.

Part 3

Flow direction, accumulation and streams

Turning a grid of elevations into flow paths, drainage areas and a stream network

Flow direction grid (D8)

  1. Recondition
  2. Fill sinks
  3. Flow direction
  4. Flow accum.
  5. Stream definition
  6. Segmentation
  7. Catchments
  8. Raster → vector
Key idea

Each cell drains to its steepest downslope neighbor, stored as a single direction code.

Direction codes (powers of 2)

32NW64N128NE
16Wcell1E
8SW4S2SE

Water in the center cell leaves toward the neighbor with the matching code, e.g. 1 = east, 4 = south.

This grid is the basis for

Flow accumulation, stream delineation and watershed boundaries

Limitation

One flow path per cell, so flow cannot split. D-infinity allows multiple directions (not covered here).

Display tip

In ArcGIS a flow-direction raster often looks like a hillshade, because each code matches a slope aspect.

Flow direction grid: arrows to codes

  1. Recondition
  2. Fill sinks
  3. Flow direction
  4. Flow accum.
  5. Stream definition
  6. Segmentation
  7. Catchments
  8. Raster → vector
Key idea

The same 5 × 5 grid shown two ways: arrows (left) and the D8 codes stored in the raster (right).

How to read it

Match each arrow to the code legend at the top. The cell in the same position on the right holds that code.

Try it

  • Top-left cell: arrow points southeast → 2
  • Middle row, first cell: arrow points northeast → 128
  • Bottom-right cell: arrow points west → 16

Why codes?

A raster stores numbers, not arrows. Powers of 2 give each direction a unique value that tools can decode.

Grid network

  1. Recondition
  2. Fill sinks
  3. Flow direction
  4. Flow accum.
  5. Stream definition
  6. Segmentation
  7. Catchments
  8. Raster → vector
Key idea

Connect every cell to its downstream neighbor and the flow directions become a connected network.

Read the figure

  • Left: each cell's flow-direction arrow
  • Right: the same arrows joined cell-center to cell-center

What to notice

  • Every cell has exactly one downstream link (D8)
  • Paths converge as you move downstream, just like tributaries

Why it matters

This network lets GIS trace water from any cell to the outlet, and count how many cells drain through each cell. That count is flow accumulation, next.

Flow accumulation grid

  1. Recondition
  2. Fill sinks
  3. Flow direction
  4. Flow accum.
  5. Stream definition
  6. Segmentation
  7. Catchments
  8. Raster → vector
Key idea

Flow accumulation counts the number of upstream cells that drain into each cell, a proxy for drainage area.

Read the figure

Left: the grid network with each cell's count. Right: the same counts as a raster. The outlet cell (24) collects flow from all 24 other cells in the 5 × 5 grid.

Interpreting values

  • 0: ridges and high points (nothing drains in)
  • High values: channels

Worked example

On a 30 m DEM each cell is 900 m². A value of 24 means 24 × 900 = 21,600 m² ≈ 2.16 ha of contributing area.

Used to find stream initiation points and estimate runoff volume.

Flow accumulation > 5 cell threshold

  1. Recondition
  2. Fill sinks
  3. Flow direction
  4. Flow accum.
  5. Stream definition
  6. Segmentation
  7. Catchments
  8. Raster → vector
Key idea

A threshold turns the continuous accumulation raster into stream vs. non-stream cells.

Read the figure

Outlined cells meet the threshold: 5, 11, 15, 24. These become stream cells. Low values (0–3) are hillslopes and ridges.

Note that the cell with exactly 5 is included, so the rule in this figure behaves as “5 or more”.

Hydrologic meaning

The threshold is the minimum drainage area needed to start a channel. It depends on DEM resolution, terrain and climate.

Why it is tied to Q

Accumulation is a stand-in for drainage area, so it links directly to channel initiation and stream discharge (Q).

Stream network for 5 cell threshold drainage area

  1. Recondition
  2. Fill sinks
  3. Flow direction
  4. Flow accum.
  5. Stream definition
  6. Segmentation
  7. Catchments
  8. Raster → vector
Key idea

Streams emerge where enough upstream area concentrates flow. GIS models this with accumulation + connectivity.

Read the figure

The threshold cells (11, 15, 5, 24) are linked by their flow directions into a continuous downstream path (red line): a channel.

Two ingredients

  • Accumulation picks which cells are streams
  • Flow direction connects them into a network

Sensitivity to the threshold

  • Lower threshold → denser network, more small tributaries
  • Higher threshold → simplified network

Streams with a 200 cell threshold

  1. Recondition
  2. Fill sinks
  3. Flow direction
  4. Flow accum.
  5. Stream definition
  6. Segmentation
  7. Catchments
  8. Raster → vector
Key idea

A higher threshold keeps only channels with a large contributing area: fewer, better-defined streams.

The numbers

200 cells × 900 m² = 180,000 m² = 18 ha (about 44 acres)

Effect on the network

  • Small headwater streams are removed
  • Network focuses on the main channels
  • Better matches perennial or larger streams

In practice

Stream networks are model representations, not exact reality. The threshold is often calibrated against field data or mapped hydrography.

Watershed draining to outlet

  1. Recondition
  2. Fill sinks
  3. Flow direction
  4. Flow accum.
  5. Stream definition
  6. Segmentation
  7. Catchments
  8. Raster → vector
Key idea

A watershed is every cell that drains to a chosen outlet. Move the outlet and the whole watershed changes.

Read the figure

  • Bright red cell (lower right): the outlet
  • Shaded cells: drainage cells leading to the outlet
  • Orange line: the watershed boundary (topographic divide)

How it's computed

Starting at the outlet, the flow direction grid is traced upstream. Only cells hydrologically connected to the outlet are included.

Not every nearby cell is in the watershed. The boundary follows the high points that separate it from neighboring watersheds.

Watershed and drainage paths delineated from a 30 m DEM

  1. Recondition
  2. Fill sinks
  3. Flow direction
  4. Flow accum.
  5. Stream definition
  6. Segmentation
  7. Catchments
  8. Raster → vector
Key idea

The automated method is more consistent than hand delineation.

Compare this with the hand-digitized watershed in Part 2: it is the same map area.

Read the figure

  • Purple line: watershed boundary
  • Blue lines: drainage paths (flow paths)
  • Red dot: outlet

Why automation matters

  • Reproducible: the same DEM gives the same answer
  • Reduces the subjectivity of reading contours

Small differences from hand-drawn boundaries usually appear in flat areas or where contours are subtle.

Q7 A cell has a flow direction code of 8. In which direction does water leave it?

Southwest.

Q8 On a 10 m DEM a cell has a flow accumulation of 50. What contributing area does that represent?

Each cell is 10 × 10 = 100 m², so 50 × 100 = 5,000 m² (0.5 ha).

Q9 What happens to the stream network if you lower the threshold from 200 cells to 50 cells?

A denser network with many more small headwater tributaries (and more, smaller catchments).

Q10 Why does moving the outlet change the entire watershed, not just the area near the outlet?

A watershed is every cell that drains to the outlet. A new outlet changes which upstream cells are connected to it.

Part 4

Preparing the DEM

Pits, peaks and reconditioning. In practice these steps come first; they make sense once you've seen how flow routing works.

The pit removal problem

  1. Recondition
  2. Fill sinks
  3. Flow direction
  4. Flow accum.
  5. Stream definition
  6. Segmentation
  7. Catchments
  8. Raster → vector
Key idea

Pit removal is the first thing done with a DEM. Unfilled pits trap flow and break the network.

What is a pit?

A set of one or more cells with no downstream cells around it. Water gets trapped instead of flowing out.

Why pits occur

DEM creation produces artificial pits:

  • Interpolation errors
  • Limited resolution or data noise

Why they matter

Unless removed, pits become sinks that:

  • Break flow connectivity
  • Isolate parts of the watershed
  • Corrupt flow accumulation and streams

The peak removal problem

  1. Recondition
  2. Fill sinks
  3. Flow direction
  4. Flow accum.
  5. Stream definition
  6. Segmentation
  7. Catchments
  8. Raster → vector
Key idea

DEMs can also contain artificial peaks: cells that are unrealistically high.

What is a peak?

A spurious cell with elevation greater than expected given the trend of the surrounding surface. Often caused by interpolation noise.

Why peaks matter

  • Misdirect flow away from true channels
  • Create incorrect flow directions
  • Shift watershed boundaries

Correction

Peaks are reduced or smoothed to match surrounding elevation trends.

Pit filling and peak removal together give a hydrologically realistic surface.

Pit and peak filling

  1. Recondition
  2. Fill sinks
  3. Flow direction
  4. Flow accum.
  5. Stream definition
  6. Segmentation
  7. Catchments
  8. Raster → vector
Key idea

Increase elevation to the pour point elevation until the pit drains to a neighbor.

  1. Find the pitLocate cells with no downstream neighbor.
  2. Raise the cellsIncrease the pit's elevation step by step.
  3. Stop at the pour pointThe final elevation equals the pit's lowest outlet, so water can now flow to a neighbor.

Peaks

Lower or smooth elevated cells to match the surrounding terrain.

The principle

Adjust the DEM minimally: just enough for continuous flow, while preserving the overall terrain shape.

Effect of pit filling on elevation

  1. Recondition
  2. Fill sinks
  3. Flow direction
  4. Flow accum.
  5. Stream definition
  6. Segmentation
  7. Catchments
  8. Raster → vector
Key idea

Filling raises depressions to their pour point, creating a continuous downstream gradient.

Read the profile

  • Original surface (blue) vs. filled surface (pink)
  • Flat “steps” mark where pits were filled

Hydrologic impact

  • Removes artificial storage
  • Lets water flow continuously downstream

The tradeoff

Filling slightly alters the true terrain, but it is necessary for correct flow routing.

DEM reconditioning

  1. Recondition
  2. Fill sinks
  3. Flow direction
  4. Flow accum.
  5. Stream definition
  6. Segmentation
  7. Catchments
  8. Raster → vector
Key idea

Reconditioning adjusts the DEM so modeled flow paths line up with mapped streams.

  1. Step 1Take a mapped stream network and a DEM
  2. Step 2Make a grid (raster) of the streams
  3. Step 3Raise the off-stream DEM cells by an arbitrary elevation increment
  4. Step 4Result: “burned-in” DEM streams = mapped streams

Why it's needed

DEMs don't always capture channel locations, especially in flat areas or with low-resolution data.

What it improves

  • Accuracy of flow direction and flow accumulation
  • Modeled drainage matches observed hydrography

“Burning in” the streams

  1. Recondition
  2. Fill sinks
  3. Flow direction
  4. Flow accum.
  5. Stream definition
  6. Segmentation
  7. Catchments
  8. Raster → vector
Key idea

Burning in forces flow to follow mapped channels, eliminating errors where the DEM misplaces streams.

How

  • Lower the elevation along stream paths, or
  • Raise the surrounding cells relative to the streams

Especially important for

  • Flat terrain
  • Low-resolution DEMs
  • Areas where channels are not well defined in the elevation data

AGREE elevation grid modification methodology

  1. Recondition
  2. Fill sinks
  3. Flow direction
  4. Flow accum.
  5. Stream definition
  6. Segmentation
  7. Catchments
  8. Raster → vector
Key idea

AGREE is a surface reconditioning system that makes the DEM consistent with vector hydrography.

Read the figure

  • Plan (top): black cells = stream delineated from the original DEM; grey cells = the known stream location, which the modified DEM now reproduces
  • Section A–A (bottom): original vs. modified elevation across the valley

How it differs from simple burning

Elevations are changed near the streams with smooth transitions, preserving the overall terrain shape and avoiding abrupt, unrealistic changes.

AGREE parameters

  1. Recondition
  2. Fill sinks
  3. Flow direction
  4. Flow accum.
  5. Stream definition
  6. Segmentation
  7. Catchments
  8. Raster → vector
Key idea

AGREE combines smooth interpolation (realistic slopes) with sharp enforcement (clear channels).

Three settings control how the DEM is changed around each stream line. Larger buffers give a wider, smoother adjustment zone.

Stream buffer

Number of cells around the linear feature over which smoothing occurs.

Smooth drop/raise

Vertical units the river is dropped (positive) or extruded (negative). Used to interpolate the DEM into the buffered area.

Sharp drop/raise

Additional vertical units the linear feature itself is dropped or extruded, on top of the smooth interpolation, to preserve the line used for burning/fencing.

AGREE procedure

  1. Recondition
  2. Fill sinks
  3. Flow direction
  4. Flow accum.
  5. Stream definition
  6. Segmentation
  7. Catchments
  8. Raster → vector
Key idea

In short: enforce the stream location, smooth the surrounding terrain, reinforce the flow path.

  1. Adjust the stream cellsDrop (or raise) the elevation of the cells corresponding to the vector lines by a set amount, so the streams act as the main flow paths.
  2. Buffer the vector linesDefine the zone around each stream where the terrain will be modified. This controls how far the adjustment extends.
  3. Smooth the surrounding terrainAssign elevations inside the buffer so there is a straight-line path from the vector line to the original elevation just outside the buffer.
  4. Reinforce the streamDrop (or raise) the stream cells by an additional amount (the sharp drop) so the channel stays clearly defined.

Check your understanding

Answer in your own words first, then open the answer to check.

Q11 What is a pit in a DEM, and what happens to flow accumulation if pits are not filled?

One or more cells with no downstream neighbor. Flow is trapped there, accumulation stops, and downstream areas are cut off.

Q12 When a pit is filled, to what elevation is it raised?

To the pour point elevation, the pit's lowest outlet, so it can drain to a neighbor.

Q13 How does AGREE differ from simply burning streams into a DEM?

Burning applies a uniform raise or drop. AGREE uses a buffer with smooth interpolation plus a sharp drop at the stream, preserving terrain shape.

Q14 In AGREE, what is the difference between the smooth and the sharp drop/raise values?

Smooth: gradual change interpolated across the buffer. Sharp: an extra drop applied to the stream cells themselves.

Part 5

From grids to features

Breaking the stream network into links, and pairing every link with the land that drains to it

Stream segments

  1. Recondition
  2. Fill sinks
  3. Flow direction
  4. Flow accum.
  5. Stream definition
  6. Segmentation
  7. Catchments
  8. Raster → vector
Key idea

The stream network is broken into segments (links), the building blocks for hydrologic analysis.

What defines a segment?

  • The stretch of stream between two junctions, or
  • Between a junction and the outlet

Read the figure

Each color is a different segment. Junctions (confluences) mark where segments begin and end.

Why segment?

Each segment gets a unique ID, which lets us:

  • Track flow through the network
  • Link streams to their catchments
  • Build routing models

Stream links in a cell network

  1. Recondition
  2. Fill sinks
  3. Flow direction
  4. Flow accum.
  5. Stream definition
  6. Segmentation
  7. Catchments
  8. Raster → vector
Key idea

Each stream cell is labeled with its link ID, turning a continuous stream into a structured network.

Read the figure

  • Left: stream cells colored by segment
  • Right: the same cells labeled 1, 2, 3 …

What the IDs allow

  • Track connectivity: which link flows into which
  • Build network topology
  • Link each segment to its catchment

Think of it like assigning IDs to road segments in a transportation network.

Stream links grid for the San Marcos subbasin

  1. Recondition
  2. Fill sinks
  3. Flow direction
  4. Flow accum.
  5. Stream definition
  6. Segmentation
  7. Catchments
  8. Raster → vector
Key idea

In a real basin, each link has a unique identifying number stored in the GIS database.

What you're seeing

A stream link network derived from a DEM. Each colored line is one link, so the network is many connected segments rather than one continuous stream.

Why it's useful

  • Tracks upstream–downstream relationships
  • Supports flow routing in hydrologic models
  • Links each segment to its own catchment

Each segment can store attributes like flow, slope or contributing area.

Stream vectorization

  1. Recondition
  2. Fill sinks
  3. Flow direction
  4. Flow accum.
  5. Stream definition
  6. Segmentation
  7. Catchments
  8. Raster → vector
Key idea

Grid stream cells are converted into vector polylines, one line per stream segment.

Read the figure

The Identify windows show that the raster's grid code is carried over as an attribute of the vector stream.

Key linkage

Raster stream ID → attribute of the vector stream

Why vectors?

  • Easier to analyze and visualize
  • Support network analysis: length, connectivity, routing
  • Required by many hydrologic and hydraulic models

Drainage points

  1. Recondition
  2. Fill sinks
  3. Flow direction
  4. Flow accum.
  5. Stream definition
  6. Segmentation
  7. Catchments
  8. Raster → vector
Key idea

DrainagePoints mark where water exits each catchment.

DrainageLines

Drawn through the centers of the cells on the stream links. They represent each segment's flow path.

DrainagePoints

Located at the centers of the outlet cells of the catchments, usually the downstream end of a stream link.

Read the figure

The inset zooms in on the cell-based stream. The points sit where flow from an upstream area converges and continues downstream.

Catchments for stream links

  1. Recondition
  2. Fill sinks
  3. Flow direction
  4. Flow accum.
  5. Stream definition
  6. Segmentation
  7. Catchments
  8. Raster → vector
Key idea

A catchment is the area that drains directly to a single stream link: one link, one catchment.

What is a catchment?

The smallest hydrologic unit in this workflow: all land draining directly to one link.

Read the figure

Each colored area is a different catchment. The arrows show that a stream link and its catchment share the same cell value.

Key relationship

  • One-to-one connection between link and catchment
  • All cells in a catchment share the same grid value (ID)

So all water in that area flows to the same stream segment.

Raster zones and vector polygons

  1. Recondition
  2. Fill sinks
  3. Flow direction
  4. Flow accum.
  5. Stream definition
  6. Segmentation
  7. Catchments
  8. Raster → vector
Key idea

Catchments go from raster zones to vector polygons: same hydrology, new format.

Raster zones (left)

Groups of cells with the same GridCode. Each zone is a catchment.

Vector polygons (right)

The same areas as polygon features, each with a matching GridID.

One-to-one

Each raster zone becomes exactly one polygon, e.g. zone 3 → polygon 3.

Catchments

  1. Recondition
  2. Fill sinks
  3. Flow direction
  4. Flow accum.
  5. Stream definition
  6. Segmentation
  7. Catchments
  8. Raster → vector
Key idea

For every stream segment there is a corresponding catchment.

What catchments represent

Representations of landscape drainage determined by a set of physical rules: gravity-driven flow, expressed through flow direction and accumulation. They are not arbitrary boundaries.

Read the figure

Each colored polygon is a catchment; blue lines are the stream segments they drain to.

What this enables

  • Runoff, sediment or pollutant contributions calculated per segment
  • Distributed hydrologic modeling

Delineation features

  1. Recondition
  2. Fill sinks
  3. Flow direction
  4. Flow accum.
  5. Stream definition
  6. Segmentation
  7. Catchments
  8. Raster → vector
Key idea

Three feature classes together represent land–water connectivity.

Catchments polygons
Contributing area for each stream segment
DrainageLines lines
The stream network and flow paths
DrainagePoints points
Outlets where flow exits each catchment

How they connect

Each catchment drains to a DrainagePoint, and that point connects to a DrainageLine. The zoomed view shows this chain.

Adjoint catchments

  1. Recondition
  2. Fill sinks
  3. Flow direction
  4. Flow accum.
  5. Stream definition
  6. Segmentation
  7. Catchments
  8. Raster → vector
Key idea

An adjoint catchment is the remaining upstream area draining to a catchment outlet.

Catchment vs. adjoint catchment

  • Catchment: area draining to a single stream segment
  • Adjoint catchment: combines all upstream catchments, the cumulative drainage area at a point

Read the figure

The highlighted area (green, upper right) shows land draining to a selected outlet, including local and upstream contributions.

Why it matters

Used to calculate total flow at a point, and for watershed-scale analysis.

Check your understanding

Answer in your own words first, then open the answer to check.

Q15 What marks the start and end of a stream segment (link)?

Junctions (confluences), or a junction and the outlet.

Q16 What is the relationship between a stream link and its catchment, and how is it preserved when catchments are converted to polygons?

One-to-one: each link has one catchment sharing its ID. The raster GridCode becomes the polygon's GridID.

Q17 How is an adjoint catchment different from a catchment?

A catchment drains to one segment; an adjoint catchment is all the remaining upstream area draining to that catchment's outlet (cumulative).

Part 6

Hydrologic units and wrap-up

How small drainage units nest into larger ones, and the full processing sequence

Hydrologic units: catchment, subwatershed, watershed

Key idea

Hydrologic systems are nested: small drainage units build into larger ones through the stream network.

From smallest to largest

  • Catchments: drain to individual stream segments
  • Subwatersheds: groups of catchments draining to intermediate outlets (junctions)
  • Watershed: the entire area draining to a main outlet

Good to know

A watershed outlet can lie inside a catchment, e.g. at a USGS stream-gaging site.

Nesting supports multi-scale analysis at different levels of detail.

Hydrologic Unit Codes (HUCs)

Outside of Arc Hydro, but the standard inside the United States.

Key idea

HUCs are nested drainage areas: each level adds 2 digits, and more digits means a smaller, more detailed unit.

Follow one example down the hierarchy

  1. Region · HUC217Pacific Northwest
  2. Subregion · HUC41706Lower Snake
  3. Basin · HUC6170601Lower Snake
  4. Subbasin · HUC817060102Imnaha River
  5. Watershed · HUC101706010201Upper Imnaha River
  6. Subwatershed · HUC12170601020101North Fork Imnaha River

Summary of key processing steps

Key idea

The full Arc Hydro sequence: prepare the DEM, derive flow, define streams, delineate areas, convert to features.

Prepare the DEM

  1. DEM reconditioning
  2. Pit removal (fill sinks)

Derive flow

  1. Flow direction
  2. Flow accumulation

Define the drainage system

  1. Stream definition (threshold)
  2. Stream segmentation (links)

Delineate areas

  1. Catchment grid delineation

Convert to GIS features

  1. Raster to vector: catchment polygons, DrainageLines, catchment outlet points

Lab 3: a more detailed list of steps is in the Lab 3 Arc Hydro assignment description on Canvas.

Check your understanding

Answer in your own words first, then open the answer to check.

Q18 Order these from smallest to largest: watershed, catchment, subwatershed.

Catchment → subwatershed → watershed.

Q19 How many digits does a HUC subbasin code have? Give the example from the table.

8 digits, e.g. 17060102, Imnaha River.

Q20 Why does DEM reconditioning and pit filling come before flow direction in the workflow?

Flow direction needs a continuous surface: pits would trap flow and misplaced channels would misroute it.
